Title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
Author(s): Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang, Feixiang Ruan, Ruiyang Si, Chuanrui Zhang, Yuxuan Chen, Hao Chen, Yichen Liu, Yintianrun Zhang, Yufan Deng, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou
Abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.

Title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
Author(s): Thao Nguyen, Robert G. Alberstein, Ewa Nowara, Homa MohammadiPeyhani, Holly R. Steach, Sarah A. Robinson, Yuval Shechter, Donald W. Lee, Jason A. Vander Heiden, Franziska Seeger, Andrew Leaver-Fay, Richard Bonneau, Joshua Yao-Yu Lin
Abstract:
Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories.
  We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization.
  We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.

Title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
Author(s): Rui Qiao, Lei Xin, Baozhen Shan
Abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within +/-0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our software has three modules, each with exactly one job: a precursor mass finder recovers the accurate precursor mass from MS1, the CRF finds the peptides that fit the precursor mass by exact k-best decoding, and two BiGRU rerankers add sequence context and internal-fragment evidence. The model has 310k parameters and trains in about 17 GPU-hours. On seven held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets published in 2026 (126,262 labeled spectra), NovoCRF's mean peptide recall is 42.4%, against 39.1% for Casanovo v5 with five beams, and its amino-acid recall 64.0% against 53.1%, at 1,746 spectra/s on 18 CPU threads, 55x Casanovo's throughput on a GPU. Split by fragment evidence, NovoCRF leads on labels with up to three peptide bonds without a b or y ion, and Casanovo only beyond. NovoCRF can also search modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: it finds 32.1% of the hydroxyproline peptides of a lion bone sample.

Title: Post-stratified importance sampling
Author(s): Yuling Yao, Sergei Tikhonov
Abstract: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

Title: PLANTEUR: A Crop-Type Segmentation Benchmark for Tropical Regions
Author(s): Piper Wolters, Gabriel Tseng, Favyen Bastani, Joseph Redmon, Yawen Zhang, Hadrien Sablon, Ando Shah
Abstract: We introduce PLANTEUR, a benchmark for crop-type mapping from satellite images in the French overseas territories. Building on the PASTIS design, PLANTEUR provides georeferenced and aligned Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, and Landsat-8 sequences with parcel-derived labels spanning six tropical regions and an 8-class label space. We define both a standard test split and a leave-one-island-out protocol to measure cross-territory generalization, and evaluate fully supervised models, linear probes, and fine-tuned foundation models. The benchmark code and data are open source and available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

Title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
Author(s): João Matos, Ben Van Calster, Richard D. Riley, Paula Dhiman, Gary S. Collins
Abstract: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.

Title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
Author(s): Juan Guevara, Riccardo De Santi, Andreas Krause, Raul Astudillo
Abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

Title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
Author(s): Daniel Aibinder, Azmi Haider, Dan Rosenbaum
Abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

Title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
Author(s): Javal Vyas, Mehmet Mercang{ö}z
Abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

Title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
Author(s): Niall Jeffrey, Benjamin D. Wandelt
Abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.

Title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
Author(s): Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
Abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

Title: Creating Power Flexibility in Datacenters via Query Routing
Author(s): Shivam Patel, Bingqing Chen, Jared Fernandez, Guannan Qu, Gauri Joshi
Abstract: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.

Title: Do Ray-Traced Cities Make a Better Channel Prior for an Unseen Site? A Pre-Registered Study in Simulation, and a Test on Measured Channels that Reverses It
Author(s): Krish Patel
Abstract: Channel estimators at a newly deployed base station usually start from 3GPP stochastic channel models, which describe no particular street. We ask whether a channel prior pooled from many ray-traced cities serves an unseen site better than the 3GPP CDL models, and whether learned estimators make the difference. With Sionna RT on 14 city scenes, LMMSE estimation from covariance priors, leave-one-city-out evaluation, and pass/fail bars written down before each main experiment, we find in simulation that the pooled prior sits about 0.6 dB from a site-trained estimator with no site measurements, about what CDL reaches after 50 measurements. Learned models added little: at most 0.65 dB in estimation, and in channel prediction a simple classical method beat CNN predictors by 1.8-12 dB from 2 ms ahead. On measured channels from the DICHASUS outdoor dataset (1.272 GHz, three 2x8 arrays on one building) the result reversed: the pooled ray-traced prior was 3.2-4.1 dB worse than CDL. The simulated channels were too clean; with users at the real distances, even a scattering level tuned from 50 site measurements left the prior about 2 dB behind CDL. A pre-registered follow-on on two more measured environments found the generic CDL prior 2.1-4.7 dB from a site-trained one: no further in a factory hall than on the street, furthest in a small lab room. Finally, a hallway model calibrated to measurements by differentiable ray tracing reproduced delay spread, but as a prior in an unmeasured part of the hallway it was 4.5 dB worse than CDL on the full array. All measured results come from one sounder.

Title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
Author(s): Po-Yi Wu, Djengo Cyun-Jyun Fang, Dian Cheng, Tsung-Wei Ke
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/

Title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
Author(s): Eoin Quinn, Oliver Bent
Abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.

Title: LLMs as MDP Designers: A Dependency-Aware Agentic Framework for Automated Robot Policy Generation
Author(s): Hong Je-Gal, Jinwoo Kim, Chanbin Yi, Hyun-Suk Lee
Abstract: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.

Title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
Author(s): Sofia Blyufer, Amir Kleiner, Uri Peskin
Abstract: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.

Title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
Author(s): Jin Zhu, Junxian Zhu
Abstract: Variable selection is an important task for interpreting potentially complex systems in fields such as biology, business, and sociology. The importance of variable selection has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we are mainly interested in model-agnostic variable selection for identifying variables that have general nonlinear dependence on the response. We propose MambaPFN, short for Model-Agnostic Markov BlAnket selection with Prior-data Fitted Networks, which is built upon the Transformer, a building block of many popular large language models. Specifically, we consider a functional-mapping perspective on variable-selection learning, in which the Transformer is treated as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables. To learn this mapping, MambaPFN introduces three new components: (i) a faithful, rich, and scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, (ii) an objective that targets each variable's posterior inclusion probability, and (iii) a modified Transformer architecture tailored to variable selection. Once pretrained, MambaPFN is applied to new datasets without parameter updates. Empirically, MambaPFN achieves desirable variable-selection performance in simulation studies and exhibits a scaling law---more pretraining datasets and larger models can continuously improve its performance. Applied to a Facebook comments dataset, MambaPFN selects the fewest variables and achieves the highest computational efficiency and predictive performance, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.

Title: HTCE: Homeomorphism-inspired Topological Cross-Scene Experience Canonicalization and Reuse for Object Navigation
Author(s): Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu
Abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git

Title: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
Author(s): Shibo Feng, Wei Li, Min Wu, Chunyan Miao, Peilin Zhao
Abstract: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/William-Liwei/uniflow

Title: Reconstructing Fraudulent Strategies in Online Payments via Interpretable Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Author(s): Huilin He, Weiyu Han, Linbo Shao, Ruobing Zuo, Xiao Tan, Shuai Chen, Dawei Cheng
Abstract: Payment fraud causes financial losses and undermines users' trust in web payment services. Although fraud detection is a critical defense for payment security, complex and diverse fraudulent behaviors can still evade detection. Generating fraud samples for data augmentation can broaden detectors' coverage of different fraud patterns. However, existing methods matching the distribution of transaction attributes alone do not ensure that generated sequences preserve the sequential relationships among transaction choices, payment feedback, and subsequent behavioral adjustments. To this end, we propose PaySeqGen, an interpretable inverse reinforcement learning framework that reconstructs fraud behavior policies from fraudsters' observed payment trajectories. We design a mechanism for constructing candidate actions to support plausible payment sequence generation while enabling exploration. The framework also learns interpretable behavioral rewards that capture fraudsters' preferences across different transaction contexts. By alternating between reward learning and policy optimization, the framework reconstructs policies that generate new fraud sequences for detector augmentation and learns interpretable rewards supporting sequential fraud-pattern analysis in real trajectories. Experiments in real-world payment scenarios at Ant International, a leading global digital payment provider, show that PaySeqGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods. Reward-based trajectory analysis also identifies fraud patterns of practical value, helping analyst locating suspicious segments and examine multistep fraud tactics. Evaluation in the deployed system of online payment further confirms its effectiveness.

Title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
Author(s): Alejandro Mayorga-Redondo, José Daniel Viqueira, Diego Alvarez-Estevez, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey, Andrés Gómez
Abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.

Title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
Author(s): Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

Title: Kierston & KierstonBench: Simulation of Allentown, PA and Evaluation of Language Models in Crime Investigation and Surveillance Tasks
Author(s): Andrew Semenov, Svyatoslav Dorofeev
Abstract: Large language models are candidates for collecting and analyzing records in criminal investigations and mass surveillance. Their capability and accuracy in this work cannot currently be measured. Real deployments lack the ground truth needed to score a model's conclusions, and no benchmark evaluates these capabilities in a simulated environment. We present Kierston, a city-scale simulation engine, and KierstonBench, a benchmark that tests these capabilities against known simulated events. Kierston models approximately 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, generating their daily activities and the telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records that surveillance and investigative systems collect about them. These records derive from a common behavioral timeline and are distributed across sources representing separate providers. Models investigate through a restricted records interface, linking observations across sources without access to the underlying simulation. The benchmark comprises 32 task families covering record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation and assessment of deceptive accounts. In an evaluation of sixteen language models, most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support. A small number of frontier models solved most of the tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient. In some cases these models still fell for common deceptions and assumptions, and none replaced an investigator.

Title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
Author(s): Raz Marshanski, Liran Nochumsohn, Mayank Jauhari, Boris N. Oreshkin, Omri Azencot
Abstract: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25$\times$ reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.

Title: Feature-Based and Deep Learning Methods for Astronomical Light Curve Classification
Author(s): V. Baymakanov, Kh. Khamitov, A. Raimova, A. Isaeva, R. Taran, M. Zedan, M. Kornilov, M. Demianenko, K. Malanchev, M. Hushchyn
Abstract: We compare feature-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning for variable star classification using the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) StarEmbed dataset, which contains about 40,000 objects across seven imbalanced classes. Classical models trained on physically motivated features consistently outperform deep networks trained directly on raw light curves. We find that limited labeled data contributes to the performance gap, while the multivariate, irregularly sampled, and morphologically diverse nature of light curves poses additional challenges for deep learning models. While deep learning holds promise for learning representations directly from observations, our results indicate that current models fail to generalize with the available training set size. These findings motivate further investigation of the benefits of scaling labeled datasets and self-supervised pretraining on large unlabeled surveys. This work establishes a quantitative baseline for future research and highlights the need for further innovations to unlock the potential of deep learning in astronomical time series analysis.

Title: SAT Encoding for Set of At-Most-K Cardinality Constraints with Ladder Shape
Author(s): Hieu Truong Xuan, Tuyen Kieu Van, Khanh To Van
Abstract: This paper presents a novel SAT encoding designed to represent a sequence of At-Most-K cardinality constraints arranged in a ladder-like structure, referred to as the Ladder AMK constraint. These AMK constraints feature a ladder-like arrangement, with shared common variables in the center and two variables differing at the beginning and the end. The proposed encoding first decomposes the sequence of AMK constraints into separated blocks, then encodes each block as a whole rather than encoding each AMK constraint individually. This approach improves the efficiency of constraint solving in SAT solvers by significantly reducing the size of the encoding, precisely the number of variables, and the generated clauses required. To achieve this, the encoding employs Sequential Counter to encode each block and constructs clauses that link adjacent blocks, ensuring equivalence with the input constraints. Compared to the previously proposed encoding that uses BDD for Ladder AMO constraint, our encoding requires fewer variables and clauses. Our study is the first study that develops SAT encoding for Ladder AMK constraints with k>1. Experimental results on single Ladder AMO and Ladder AMK constraints indicate that our encoding significantly enhances both the size of the encoding and the efficiency of solving time compared to existing encodings. Furthermore, by evaluating on the two real-world combinatorial problems, namely Anti-bandwidth Problem and Nurse Rostering Problem, we found that the proposed encoding surpasses alternative encodings, as well as more advanced Constraint Programming and Mixed Integer Programming solvers. In summary, the SAT encoding technique presented in this paper provides a more efficient method for encoding sequence constraint, specifically Ladder AMK constraint, which could enhance the effectiveness of SAT solving for various problems involving this type of constraint.

Title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
Author(s): Andrea Cenzato, Lukas Karch, Andre Luckow, Yoran Pichon, Francesco Pasqua, Abouzar Ghasemi, Rishikesh Ranade, Ira Shokar, Julia Kowalski
Abstract: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

Title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
Author(s): Jimmy Wang, Yifan Chou, Kaifeng Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Binghao Huang, Tao Yu, Saleh Nabi, Yunzhu Li
Abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.

Title: Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Optimization for UAV-Assisted NOMA-MEC Systems
Author(s): Yaxuan Jiao, Jiaxuan Lv, Jyoti Sahni, Wuyungerile Li, Winston K. G. Seah
Abstract: The integration of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), mobile edge computing (MEC) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) provides an effective solution for computation-intensive and latency-sensitive services in infrastructure-deficient environments. However, the joint optimization of UAV trajectories, task offloading, communication and computing resources under heterogeneous task priorities results in a highly coupled mixed-integer non-convex problem. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Intelligent Evolutionary Algorithm (HIEA) for priority-aware multi-UAV cooperative NOMA-MEC networks, which integrates multi-head deep Q-network (MH-DQN)-based intelligent decision generation, communication-aware initialization, adaptive evolutionary exploration and successive convex approximation (SCA)-based precision refinement. Specifically, a novel communication-aware initialization mechanism, termed Channel Quality Indicator (CQI)-guided Load-Aware Trajectory Initialization (CQI-LATI), is designed to incorporate CQI and task workload characteristics into evolutionary population construction, generating high-quality and diversity-preserving initial populations. Theoretical analysis characterizes HIEA's search-space reduction, the quality-diversity trade-off of CQI-guided initialization, and the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of SCA refinement, and extensive simulations demonstrate that HIEA outperforms benchmark schemes, with gains of up to 6.5% in throughput, 13.6% in task completion rate and 15.3% in energy efficiency.

Title: $τ$-Rec-Books: A Disclosure-Controlled Benchmark for Requirement Elicitation in Agentic Recommender Systems
Author(s): Bharath Sivaram Narasimhan, Karthik R. Narasimhan
Abstract: While conversational recommendation systems provide a more natural user interface, they face the challenge of progressively discovering a user's needs before they can recommend an item that satisfies them. To evaluate the ability of AI agents at this elicitation process, we introduce $τ$-Rec-Books, a benchmark that holds each user request fixed while varying only when the user reveals their requirements: all at the start (volunteer), one at the start and the rest when asked (mixed), or some never (hidden). A hidden requirement can be found only by proposing books and inferring it from the user's accept or reject verdicts. We generate 450 tasks over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, develop a rule-based simulated user to answer the agent, and score recommendations against catalog metadata without an LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed tasks fail mainly because agents do not ask, and when told to ask, every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks, most failures come from agents recommending a book they never proposed to the user. When told to propose first, agents only match a simple baseline that proposes popular books, and stay well below one that uses rejection to rule out possible requirements. We release the catalog pipeline, task generator, simulated user, validators, reference agents, and all agent traces at https://github.com/nbharaths/tau-rec/tree/main/data/tracks/books-wikidata-v2.

Title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
Author(s): Xin Liu, Boyuan Sun, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Song, Mingjian Zhao, Mengyu Liu
Abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + δ$, $δ\in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.

Title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
Author(s): Yeonseok Lee
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.

Title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN
Author(s): Sneihil Gopal, Fernando J. Cintron, Richard A. Rouil
Abstract: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.

Title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
Author(s): Li Zheng, Simin Chen
Abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

Title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
Author(s): Lisheng Zhang, Qingsong Li, Zinan Xie, Yanting Yang, Qikui Yang, Peng Lu, Zhican Fu, Wentao Cui, Runtong Hou, Zhengwei Xie
Abstract: Protein structure predictors reliably identify native conformations, but do not describe the continuum connecting unfolded ensembles to folded states. Here we present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework that generates C$α$ conformational ensembles at a specified folding fraction $Q$. FoldScape reconstructs three-dimensional chains through hierarchical, sliding-window regressions of one-dimensional inter-residue distances, followed by chain assembly and sampling with a rectified-flow decoder. It is trained on multi-scale coarse-grained folding trajectories and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. Across 20 human proteins (36-857 residues), at matched sample size, FoldScape covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles, robustly across proteins, order parameters and binning choices. AlphaFold 3 better anchors the immediate native vicinity, which FoldScape does not reach, making the approaches complementary. FoldScape reconstruction accuracy remains approximately constant along $Q$, from collapsed coil to near-native globule, rather than deteriorating away from the native state. A stride-one crop-and-superpose scheme extends inference to chains several times longer than a single chain-level forward pass. We also show that training trajectories resolve mechanical unfolding at residue resolution, that elongation-conditioned ensembles exhibit reproducible continuous observables across pulling velocities, and that partially unfolded chains form geometrically coherent segments. FoldScape thus combines broad coverage of folding stages with stable reconstruction accuracy, without per-protein simulation.

Title: DualWorldBench: Can Agents Plan Deliveries across Symbolic and Grounded Worlds?
Author(s): Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo
Abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.

Title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
Author(s): Megan Healy, Hossein Valavi
Abstract:
Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model.
  We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold.
  In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds.
  The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.

Title: Clocks all the way down: does sequence-processing AI need endogenous temporal structure?
Author(s): Meysam Hashemi, Alireza Valizadeh, Viktor Jirsa
Abstract: Mainstream sequence-processing AI is temporally reactive: each update is driven by input and learned state transitions, rather than by an independently evolving internal temporal reference. Biological brains, by contrast, continuously generate rhythmic activity that structures perception, memory, and cognition, and this rhythmicity reaches all the way to behavior. We ask whether this difference is merely implementational or genuinely computational. Four lines of evidence suggest that endogenous temporal structure supports putative functions that input-driven architectures may not readily replicate: 1) phase-dependent routing of information, 2) delay-structured combinatorial representation, 3) cross-frequency multiplexing of items, and 4) oscillation-gated offline consolidation. A proof-of-concept delay-ablation test dissociates representational capacity from memory retrieval. In recurrent and spatial spiking networks with fixed synaptic weights and connectivity, shuffling delays preserves part of the capacity but substantially impairs the sequence retrieval. The relative contrast is more pronounced for spatial networks and longer propagations. Instantaneous transmission collapses capacity itself. We then outline a cross-frequency multiplexing scheme that combines item identity and serial order with alternative mechanisms for selective memory retrieval. Finally, we state one falsifiable hypothesis, conditions for matched-resource tests, and three research directions: the components already exist; the disciplined comparison does not.

Title: GlucoAgent: Personalized Glucose Forecasting from Multimodal Personal Context
Author(s): Xingzhi Sun, Hyo Jin Kim, Zhiyuan Wang, Hao Chen
Abstract: Continuous glucose monitors, smartwatches, meal logs, and health profiles form a rich multimodal personal context that can significantly enhance glucose forecasting. However, existing methods struggle to effectively utilize these signals to improve glucose prediction because the relevance of different modalities varies drastically across individuals and time. We present GlucoAgent, an LLM-based agentic system that addresses this challenge through dynamic, case-by-case analysis at inference time. For each forecast, GlucoAgent writes and runs code over an individual's multimodal context and returns predictions with a reason and supporting evidence. The generated programs are highly diverse, ranging from retrieving similar past meals to fitting and back-testing physiological and statistical models. On CGMacros, a multimodal glucose dataset, GlucoAgent outperforms time series foundation models on every forecasting horizon, achieving an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL compared to 23.5 mg/dL of Chronos-2, the leading multimodal time series foundation model. Furthermore, GlucoAgent is highly effective at leveraging multimodal data. The addition of multimodal data reduces its average RMSE by 1.4 mg/dL (24.0 mg/dL to 22.5 mg/dL), compared to a marginal 0.3 mg/dL (23.8 mg/dL to 23.5 mg/dL) improvement for Chronos-2. This advantage is most pronounced in challenging post-meal windows, where GlucoAgent uses multimodal context to reduce 60-minute forecast RMSE by 4.6 mg/dL (31.0 mg/dL to 26.5 mg/dL), far exceeding the 0.8 mg/dL (31.9 mg/dL to 31.1 mg/dL) reduction achieved by Chronos-2.
